prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There is no trial evidence yet. The starting network collapses to DONE early: mean episode length is 1.6 at 25% of training and 1.0 after that. I see two likely causes. (1) Under the hidden mirror rule, the action logit for column x has to read target, build and height information from world column 8-dx-x. Two 3x3 convolutions can only see 5 columns, so they cannot learn this mapping. Because no placement can be learned, DONE (reward 0) beats random placement (negative reward). (2) The default recipe gives only 32 large updates and little exploration. Once the features are mirrored in the network, the footprint pooling in action coordinates matches the brick's real cells exactly. So a learned layer that mixes across columns, or across all cells, should be able to learn the reflection. I pair this with a recipe that has more entropy and more updates. A versus C tests 2 vs 4 PPO epochs, and A versus B tests row mixing vs whole-grid token mixing.

### Round 2
On 4 of the 6 runs, plus the starting architecture, the agent learned to press DONE before placing any brick. Training episodes were about 1 placement long by 25% of training. Only r1c3 seed 1 broke out (0.15), so the 0.076 mean is mostly seed luck. The likely cause is the mirror rule. A convolution or footprint pool sees the target at column c but must score the action at column 8-dx-c. Its early placements land in the wrong place, earn negative reward, and DONE (reward 0) wins. RowMix can learn the mirror, but it must learn it from scratch over the whole row. Flipping a learned feature map along X makes the head's footprint pool at action x cover exactly the landing columns 8-dx-x to 7-x for every brick width. Giving the head both orientations and letting it learn which to use should give a positive learning signal early. Recipe: 4 epochs with small batches (r1c3) was the only recipe that worked.

### Round 3
Every trial gets stuck at an immediate DONE unless a seed escapes it. Random placements mostly fill cells outside the target, so they earn negative reward, while DONE earns 0. Only networks that align features with the mirrored landing columns have escaped: RowMix (r1c3) and the flip-concat stem (r2c3, 0.416 on one seed). Raising entropy to 0.05 helped, but seed 0 still collapsed every time. Flipping the 1x1 stem output along X lines up action anchor x with the landing columns 8-dx-x..7-x for every footprint. The footprint pooling then covers exactly the cells a brick fills. The unflipped copy in r2c3 is misaligned and probably only adds noise, which slows the early signal that has to beat DONE. Next: keep only the flipped (fully aligned) features, test a larger batch to reduce noisy updates, and add a stem skip into the head so per-layer missing and height features reach it sharply.

### Round 4
The key finding is alignment. Any version that keeps the unflipped stem (RowMix, Mixer, concat of flipped and unflipped, or a flip only in the head) collapsed to immediate DONE in most seeds. Mirroring the learned stem features along X before the 3x3 convolutions (flip-only) made both seeds escape the collapse in every run, so later layers work in landing coordinates. With 128 envs and 2,048-sample batches, r3c2 reached 0.844 and 0.803 (mean 0.823). The small-batch run of the same network (r3c1) spread from 0.26 to 0.80, so larger batches seem to reduce seed luck. The stem skip to the head (r3c3, 0.62 against 0.53 at small batch) is within noise but may help. Training success was still rising at the end of every run, so learning is short of samples and the network should stay small. In this last round each candidate refines r3c2 with one change: the stem skip, longer credit assignment (gamma and GAE lambda), or 3 PPO epochs to collect more samples.

## Trial it ended with
name: Flip-only big batch + stem skip
hypothesis: r3c2 recipe plus the r3c3 stem skip. The footprint head also gets the flipped, unblurred per-cell stem features, so pooled max and min can match landing layers to missing cells more sharply. Large batches should keep both seeds stable. Refuted if the mean is no higher than 0.823, or if either seed drops clearly below 0.80.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 1 says: "Under the hidden mirror rule, the action logit for column x has to read target, build and height information from world column 8-dx-x."
